vignette:
He is 63, an African man who has spent most of his adult life as a journalist, someone who once believed that bearing witness was a way of keeping chaos at a distance. For decades he works in busy newsrooms and on dusty roads, interviewing grieving families, politicians, and witnesses to violence. He learns how to ask steady questions while keeping his own feelings tucked behind a notebook. He prides himself on being the calm one at home too, the husband who listens carefully, the man his relatives call when something difficult needs to be handled.

The event that changes him does not happen to him directly. It happens to his wife.

One evening, several years ago, she is caught in a brutal roadside attack while returning from a family visit. He is at work when the phone rings. At first he thinks it is another source calling late. Instead he hears a stranger’s voice, rushed and uneven, saying there has been violence, that his wife is alive, that she is being taken to the hospital. He remembers only fragments after that: his pen rolling off the desk, the newsroom lights suddenly too bright, the drive through traffic with one hand shaking on the steering wheel. He is used to arriving where bad things have already happened, but this time when he reaches the hospital corridor and sees blood on his wife’s clothing, he feels as if the floor itself tilts.

In the weeks that follow, he moves like a man assigned a story he cannot put down. He speaks to doctors, calls relatives, manages paperwork, sits beside her bed. Outwardly he is efficient. People praise how composed he is. Inside, he keeps replaying the call and the image of her face when she first sees him in the emergency room—fear, relief, and something broken open that he cannot forget. At night, when he closes his eyes, he hears the stranger’s voice and imagines all the ways she might have died before he got there. He starts sleeping in short, jagged stretches. If he dozes, he wakes drenched in sweat, heart pounding, reaching for her in the dark to make sure she is still there.

After she comes home, he becomes watchful in a way that at first seems like devotion. He insists on driving her everywhere. If she is ten minutes late, he calls again and again. He checks locks repeatedly before bed, then gets up to check them once more. The sound of tires skidding outside or raised voices in the street sends a jolt through him so strong that he has to grip the arm of his chair. He begins scanning every road for danger, every face for threat. He tells himself he is being sensible. His wife notices that his jaw is always tight.

Work, once the place where he feels most competent, becomes harder. When editors ask him to cover stories involving assault or hospitals, he finds excuses to pass them to younger reporters. On assignment, if someone describes an attack on a spouse or parent, he feels his chest constrict and his concentration slip. He still takes notes, but later he stares at them unable to shape them into copy. At times he becomes irritated with colleagues for what he privately experiences as carelessness—their jokes in the newsroom, their easy talk about “the usual violence.” He has spent years listening to other people’s trauma, but now ordinary reporting language feels almost obscene.

At home he speaks less. His wife survives, but her own recovery is uneven, and he cannot bear to ask certain questions about what she remembers. He worries that if she tells him too much, the images in his mind will become unbearable; if she tells him too little, he fills in the blanks himself. Their marriage grows quieter around the event, as if both of them walk around a fire they do not want to stir. Their adult children notice that he startles easily and no longer enjoys family gatherings. When relatives crowd the house, he smiles briefly, then slips away to sit alone on the veranda, listening for cars outside.

He says what troubles him most is that he no longer recognizes himself. He used to be a man who went toward difficult stories. Now he plans routes to avoid the road where his wife was attacked. He avoids the hospital where she was treated, even when visiting others would be expected of him. Some mornings he sits in his car outside the office, unable to get out because he has been overtaken by the memory of that phone call, his body reacting as though it is happening again. He feels ashamed of this. As a journalist, he has always believed in facts, sequence, evidence. Yet his own mind does not obey chronology. The past breaks into the present without warning.

What remains most painful for him is a persistent sense of failure. He knows, rationally, that he did not cause what happened and could not have prevented it. But he returns again and again to the thought that he should have protected her, should have been there, should have somehow known. He carries this belief quietly, beneath his professionalism and beneath his care for his wife. In sessions, he speaks gently and with precision, but whenever he describes that night, his voice thins, his eyes fix on a point in the distance, and he looks like a man still standing in a hospital corridor, waiting to learn whether the person he loves will live.
